intro_text:
Kamala Beach runs along Phuket's west coast in a subdistrict the Kathu district registry counted at 5,459 residents as of 31 March 2004, across six villages. The name comes from Sanskrit and Pali kamalā, "lotus." Wikipedia's geography entry gives the beach as a 3-kilometer curve; ground-level travel accounts put it closer to 2. Both figures describe the same strip, measured differently.

The place was a fishing settlement before it was a resort. Travel accounts of the early 1990s describe buffaloes on the sand and fishermen drying small fish on tarps behind the beach, a scatter of thatched huts, a school, a temple. The first hotels appeared around 1994. The older village survives inland, organized around the marble-fronted Kamala Mosque on Khok Yang street, still described in tourism and real-estate copy as a Muslim fishing community distinct from the resort strip along the water.

The resort strip is anchored, at its north tip, by Phuket FantaSea, a nighttime theme park that opened 20 December 1998 after a build cost of more than 3,500 million baht, then roughly $100 million. It seats 3,000 for a 70-minute show inside a reproduction Sukhothai-era elephant palace, and feeds up to 4,000 at the Golden Kinnaree Buffet Restaurant next door. On 26 December 2004 the Indian Ocean tsunami reached this coast; a surviving video from Kamala shows a restaurant's ground floor flooding, sweeping away an elderly couple. FantaSea took an estimated 60-70 million baht in damage, lost 150-200 million baht in cancelled bookings, closed 10 January 2005 in what was announced as a ten-day closure to 18 January, as visitor counts collapsed to about 15 a day, then reopened on Wednesday, 19 January 2005 — nine days later than the original 10-day estimate — with about 100 visitors at the first show, mostly foreign tourists, and continued operating from there.

South of the main beach, a dead-end lane nicknamed Millionaire Row runs past Rayee and Hua beaches to private villas, Paresa Resort and the Hyatt Regency Phuket among them, coral-fringed water too rough for swimming. It is the coastline the fishing village once held, now valued by the square meter, not the catch.

FantaSea's recent history is financial. Its operating company, Phuket FantaSea Public Company Limited (SET: PHUKET), has been rolling over bonds originally due in 2020-2021 through successive bondholder-approved extensions since the pandemic, rather than defaulting on them; its parent, Safari World Public Company (SET: SAFARI), enters the picture only as the potential recipient if one bond series converts to equity. A December 2024 meeting extended the debt's 30 December 2024 maturity by 18 months to 30 June 2026, with interest reset across three components — a 7.25 percent normal rate, 5.25 percent on remaining prior-period interest, and an additional 6.25 percent paid in three installments through 2025. That extension didn't settle the matter: a second bondholders' meeting on 15 December 2025 sought another year, to 30 June 2027, at a raised 7.50 percent rate, along with a waiver of default provisions. By April 2026 the park's schedule showed the show running three nights a week, not nightly. The beach kept doing what beaches do; the park behind it spent those years in a bondholders' meeting room in Bangkok.
spike_explainer:
Kamala's defining structure is not on the beach. It is Phuket FantaSea, a 60-acre nighttime theme park bolted onto the north end of the strip in 1998, and its trajectory from national showpiece to bond-restructuring case is the clearest single line through Kamala's last three decades.

**What was built, and what it cost.** Phuket FantaSea Public Company Limited opened its gates on 20 December 1998 after spending more than 3,500 million baht, roughly $100 million at the time, on a 60-acre site at Kamala's northern tip. The centerpiece is "Fantasy of a Kingdom," a 70-minute stage show combining illusion effects with Thai cultural staples, performed inside the Palace of the Elephants, a three-story reproduction of Sukhothai-era stone architecture seating 3,000. Next door, the Golden Kinnaree Buffet Restaurant occupies 5,220 square meters and seats up to 4,000 diners, sized among the largest buffet halls documented anywhere. A Festival Village shopping street rounds out the site. For a company built on a single asset, this was a maximalist bet on Phuket tourism holding its trajectory indefinitely upward.

**The 2004 interruption.** Six years after opening, the site met the Indian Ocean tsunami. On 26 December 2004, the wave that struck Phuket's west coast reached Kamala; one surviving amateur video shows the ground floor of a beachfront restaurant here flooding and sweeping away an elderly couple, a detail preserved in tsunami-reconnaissance archives rather than any FantaSea record. FantaSea itself, set back from the open beach, still absorbed an estimated 60 to 70 million baht in physical damage and, more seriously, 150 to 200 million baht in lost revenue as tour operators cancelled bookings through the following February, in what would ordinarily have been peak season. Daily visitor counts fell from a typical 3,000 to 6,000 to as few as 15. The park's managing director at the time, Pin Kewkacha, closed the gates on 10 January 2005 as bookings collapsed, in what was announced as a ten-day closure to 18 January, and reopened on Wednesday, 19 January 2005 — nine days later than the original 10-day estimate — with about 100 visitors at the first show, mostly foreign tourists, continuing to operate from there while pushing publicly for government-subsidized package tours to rebuild demand. The park did eventually recover, in the sense that it operated for another two decades without a comparable natural-disaster closure, even if that January reopening was not the clean ten-day turnaround sometimes described. Thailand as a whole recorded roughly 8,000 tsunami deaths that day, the great majority around Khao Lak rather than Phuket's resort beaches; Kamala's damage was real but not the region's worst.

**The 2020s interruption is different in kind.** Where the tsunami was a natural shock the park recovered from within weeks, the crisis that has occupied Phuket FantaSea's finances since the pandemic is structural. Phuket FantaSea Public Company Limited (SET: PHUKET), which operates the park, has been rolling over six separate series of bonds originally due in 2020-2021, PHUKET206A, PHUKET207A, PHUKET207B, PHUKET208A, PHUKET20DA, and PHUKET216A, through successive bondholder-approved extensions, alongside an existing 2021 debt-restructuring debenture; its parent, Safari World Public Company (stock symbol SAFARI), enters the picture only as the potential recipient if the PHUKET216A series converts to equity. On 4 December 2024, Thailand's Securities and Exchange Commission issued a public notice urging bondholders to attend a meeting five days later, in Bangkok, to vote on extending the debt's 30 December 2024 maturity by eighteen months, to 30 June 2026, with interest reset across three components: a 7.25 percent normal rate, 5.25 percent on remaining prior-period interest, and an additional 6.25 percent paid in three installments through 2025. This is not the language of a company managing routine seasonality. It is the language of a company that could not meet its obligations on schedule and needed its creditors' agreement to avoid default. That 2026 maturity didn't hold either: a second bondholders' meeting, called for 15 December 2025, asked holders to push the date another year, to 30 June 2027, raise the rate from 7.25 to 7.50 percent effective 30 December 2025, waive default provisions to permit restructuring talks with creditors, and consider converting the PHUKET216A series to equity, against 2,288.7 million baht in principal still outstanding as of 1 December 2025.

**What that means for the beach today.** The clearest visible evidence of the strain is the show schedule itself. Where a park built for 3,000 nightly guests once implied something close to daily performances, FantaSea's own listings by April 2026 showed "Fantasy of a Kingdom" running just three nights a week, Tuesday, Friday, and Sunday. A 3,000-seat theater and a 4,000-seat buffet hall, built for a tourism market that in 1998 looked like it would only grow, now operate at less than half their designed cadence. The park has not closed. Its Facebook pages, at last check, still carried five figures of followers, and travel sites still listed it as a top Kamala attraction. But the financing behind it has spent the past two years in the same kind of restructuring room that distressed Thai hospitality companies used after COVID-19 border closures, not the room a healthy 25-year-old cultural attraction is supposed to need.

**Why this is Kamala's spike, not just FantaSea's.** Kamala Beach itself is unremarkable by Phuket standards: a couple of kilometers of sand, a fishing-village core still organized around a marble mosque, a strip of resorts, a nicknamed lane of villas to the south. What distinguishes it in the historical record is that its single largest built structure is also the clearest documented case, filed with a national securities regulator rather than asserted by a travel blog, of how thin the margin is between a landmark Thai tourist attraction and a company managing default risk. The elephants on stage and the bondholders in a Bangkok conference room are, as of 2024 through the second bondholders' meeting in December 2025, the same enterprise.
honest_reckoning_note:
Most visitors who buy a ticket to "Fantasy of a Kingdom" have no reason to know they are patronizing a company that spent December 2024 asking bondholders for an 18-month extension on six separate debt series. That information sits in Thai SEC filings and a Bloomberg-style bond notice, not in the trip.com listing or the resort concierge's recommendation. The gap between what a landmark tourist attraction advertises and what its balance sheet says is normal in the industry, but Kamala is one of the few beaches where that gap is documented in a public regulatory filing rather than a rumor. The reduced three-nights-a-week show schedule in 2026 is the visible symptom; the restructuring is the cause most guests will never see. A year later, in December 2025, the company was back before bondholders asking for a second extension — another year on the maturity, a higher interest rate, a waiver of default provisions, and the potential conversion of one bond series to equity — evidence that the 2024 fix bought time rather than resolution.

The other honest problem is sourcing itself. English-language coverage of Kamala online, including its own Wikipedia article, carries a formal "unreliable sources" flag from 2021 attached specifically to claims that the beach has become a regional hub for illegal cockfighting breeding operations. The citations offered for that claim, when checked, describe police raids in Wichit and Pa Khlok, other parts of Phuket, not in Kamala itself. It is a useful case study in how confidently a specific, colorful claim about a place can circulate without actually being tied to that place, and it is why this page leaves the cockfighting claim out rather than repeat it as established fact.
reckoning_pullquote: The gap between a landmark's marketing and its balance sheet is normal; at Kamala it is on file with a securities regulator.

margin_notes.text: Phuket101's own account of pre-tourism Kamala describes buffaloes on the sand and fish drying on tarps as recently as 1990 — the resort strip is younger than most of its visitors.

The marble-fronted Kamala Mosque on Khok Yang street anchors the inland village; multiple independent tourism and real-estate sources describe Kamala as "two villages in one," the Muslim fishing community and the beachfront resort strip.

Safari World Public Company trades on the Stock Exchange of Thailand under the symbol SAFARI; its FantaSea subsidiary's bond troubles are public record, filed with Thailand's SEC, not travel-press speculation.

The beach dataset's IBTrACS record counts 7 tropical cyclone tracks passing within range of Kamala over 50 years, with a peak intensity equivalent to Category 3; wave data separately shows the roughest seas arriving July–September, the same window Thailand's monsoon season runs.
The beach's substrate is officially "unknown" in survey data; a predictive model (GloPrSM) estimates 80.3% quartz, 5.3% feldspar, 14.4% lithic grains — a modeled composition, not a measured one.
Millionaire Row's name is informal, used by travel writers rather than any official signage; it refers to the same dead-end lane serving Paresa Resort and the Hyatt Regency Phuket.

day_in_time.dawn: The beach empties out before the resort breakfast rush; boats from the older fishing families, where they still work, go out earliest, well before FantaSea's afternoon staff arrive to prep a 5:30 p.m. gate opening.
day_in_time.midday: Wave heights here run a modest annual mean of 0.73 m outside the September peak, so swimming conditions are typically calm at midday in the dry season; the Millionaire Row coves to the south stay quieter than the main strip even at peak hours.
day_in_time.golden: Late afternoon brings the FantaSea gates open (5:30 p.m.) on show nights, but by 2026 that is only Tuesday, Friday, and Sunday — the other four evenings, the northern end of the beach has no equivalent draw.
day_in_time.night: On show nights, buses and taxis converge on the FantaSea gate for the 70-minute performance and the 4,000-seat buffet; on the four nights without a show, the park's own listed hours read closed, and the strip's night life defaults to beachfront resort bars and the inland village.

food_drink.name: Golden Kinnaree Buffet Restaurant
food_drink.description: A 5,220 m² Ayutthaya-style buffet hall inside Phuket FantaSea seating up to 4,000, documented by Wikipedia as among the largest buffet restaurants anywhere; open only on the park's show nights.
food_drink.where: Inside Phuket FantaSea, Kamala's north end

food_drink.name: Kamala Market street food
food_drink.description: An informal evening market a short walk from the beach sells Thai street food, fresh produce, and clothing; sources disagree on exactly which evenings it runs (accounts variously list Monday/Friday, Tuesday/Thursday/Friday, or Tuesday/Wednesday/Sunday), suggesting the schedule shifts and shouldn't be taken as fixed.
food_drink.where: Kamala village, inland from the main beach

food_drink.name: Resort and villa dining, Millionaire Row
food_drink.description: The Hyatt Regency Phuket and Paresa Resort, among other five-star properties south of the main beach, run their own restaurant kitchens; none has a verified, independently reported signature dish distinct from standard resort Thai/international menus.
food_drink.where: Millionaire Row, south of Kamala Beach

timeline.title: Fishing village, pre-tourism
timeline.description: Travel accounts describe Kamala as a fishing settlement with buffaloes on the sand, fishermen drying small fish on tarps, thatched huts, a school, and a temple — no resort infrastructure yet in place.

timeline.title: First hotels appear
timeline.description: The earliest hotels are built near Kamala Beach, beginning the shift from fishing village to resort strip.

timeline.title: Phuket FantaSea opens
timeline.description: Phuket FantaSea Public Company Limited opens its 60-acre cultural theme park at Kamala's northern tip on 20 December 1998, after a build cost of more than 3,500 million baht (~$100 million).

timeline.title: Indian Ocean tsunami strikes
timeline.description: The 26 December 2004 tsunami reaches Kamala; a surviving video shows a beachfront restaurant's ground floor flooding and sweeping away an elderly couple. FantaSea takes an estimated 60–70 million baht in damage and 150–200 million baht in lost bookings, closing 10 January 2005 in what was announced as a ten-day closure.
timeline.source: The Thaiger, 10 Jan 2005; Wikipedia: 2004 Indian Ocean earthquake and tsunami

timeline.title: FantaSea reopens after ten-day closure
timeline.description: Phuket FantaSea reopens on Wednesday, 19 January 2005 — nine days later than the original 10-day estimate — with about 100 visitors at the first show, mostly foreign tourists, and continues operating from there; managing director Pin Kewkacha pushes for government-subsidized package tours to rebuild visitor numbers.

timeline.title: Thailand ends COVID-19 entry mandates
timeline.description: Vaccination-proof and antigen-test requirements for visiting Phuket, in place through the pandemic, are lifted on 1 October 2022.

timeline.title: SEC warns bondholders on six FantaSea debenture series
timeline.description: Thailand's Securities and Exchange Commission issues a public notice (4 Dec 2024) urging holders of six Phuket FantaSea Public Company Limited bond series, originally due in 2020-2021, to attend a 9 December meeting on extending the debt's 30 December 2024 maturity by 18 months.

timeline.title: Second bondholders' meeting seeks further extension
timeline.description: Thailand's SEC notifies holders of a second meeting on 15 December 2025 proposing to push FantaSea's bond maturity another year, from 30 June 2026 to 30 June 2027, raise interest from 7.25% to 7.50% effective 30 December 2025, waive default provisions to permit restructuring talks, and potentially convert the PHUKET216A series to equity; outstanding principal across the series stood at 2,288.7 million baht as of 1 December 2025.

timeline.title: Reduced show schedule confirmed
timeline.description: Phuket FantaSea's public listings show its "Fantasy of a Kingdom" show running three nights a week (Tuesday, Friday, Sunday) rather than nightly, the visible face of the park's ongoing financial restructuring.

zones.name: Central Kamala Beach
zones.character: The main public sand, backed by Kamala Beach Road and its resorts and restaurants; the section most travel guides mean by “Kamala Beach.”
zones.best_for: Swimming in dry season, general beach time
zones.notes: Beach length is reported as 2–3 km depending on source.

zones.name: Phuket FantaSea peninsula
zones.character: The 60-acre headland at Kamala's north end occupied by Phuket FantaSea since 1998; gated, ticketed, and now operating on a reduced 3-night-a-week schedule.
zones.notes: Operated by Phuket FantaSea Public Company Limited (SET: PHUKET), a subsidiary of Safari World Public Company (SET: SAFARI); mid-restructuring since the pandemic.

zones.name: Millionaire Row / Rayee & Hua beaches
zones.character: A dead-end lane south of the main beach serving private villas and five-star resorts (Paresa Resort, Hyatt Regency Phuket), fronting Rayee and Hua beaches where coral makes casual swimming difficult.
zones.best_for: Resort stays, coastal walking; not for casual swimming
zones.notes: “Millionaire Row” is a travel-writer nickname, not an official place name.

zones.name: Kamala village (inland)
zones.character: The older, inland core of Kamala, organized around the marble-fronted Kamala Mosque on Khok Yang street and an evening street market; the surviving Muslim fishing-village community distinct from the beachfront resort strip.
zones.notes: Subdistrict population 5,459 across 6 villages, per Kathu District registry (as of 31 Mar 2004).

landmarks.name: Phuket FantaSea
landmarks.description: A 60-acre nighttime cultural theme park at Kamala's north end, built at a cost of over 3,500 million baht; its Palace of the Elephants theater seats 3,000 for the “Fantasy of a Kingdom” show. Now operating a reduced schedule amid a multi-year bond restructuring by its operating company, Phuket FantaSea Public Company Limited (parent: Safari World Public Company).

landmarks.name: Kamala Mosque
landmarks.description: A marble-fronted mosque on Khok Yang street, the anchor of Kamala's inland Muslim fishing-village core, predating the beachfront resort development.

landmarks.name: Paresa Resort
landmarks.description: A five-star cliffside resort on Millionaire Row, the dead-end lane south of Kamala's main beach, fronting Rayee and Hua beaches.

cultural_refs.title: "Fantasy of a Kingdom" stage show
cultural_refs.creator: Phuket FantaSea Public Company Limited
cultural_refs.description: A 70-minute Thai cultural show combining illusion effects and elephant performances, staged nightly (historically) at Phuket FantaSea; by 2026 reduced to three nights a week amid the park's financial restructuring.

cultural_refs.title: 2004 Indian Ocean tsunami footage at Kamala
cultural_refs.description: Amateur video shot at Kamala on 26 December 2004 shows a beachfront restaurant's ground floor flooding and sweeping away an elderly couple; the footage is preserved in tsunami-reconnaissance archives rather than tourism material.

cultural_refs.title: Kamala Mosque and the Muslim fishing village
cultural_refs.description: Multiple independent tourism and real-estate sources describe Kamala's inland core, centered on Khok Yang street's marble mosque, as a longstanding Muslim fishing community distinct from the beachfront resort development.

recurring_events.name: "Fantasy of a Kingdom" show
recurring_events.when_text: Tuesday, Friday, and Sunday nights (as of 2026)
recurring_events.description: Phuket FantaSea's flagship 70-minute cultural show, reduced from a historically near-nightly run to three evenings a week amid the park's bond restructuring.

recurring_events.name: Kamala evening market
recurring_events.when_text: Weekday evenings, exact days vary by source

things_to_know.label: Distances are mixed straight-line and road
things_to_know.note: The nearest-city (Patong, 6.9 km) and airport (HKT, 17.8 km) figures in beach data are straight-line; by road, Patong is closer to 10 km and HKT closer to 25 km (~30 min drive).

things_to_know.label: FantaSea runs 3 nights a week, not nightly
things_to_know.note: As of a 2026 check, Phuket FantaSea's show operates Tuesday, Friday, and Sunday only; confirm the current schedule before planning a visit around it.

things_to_know.label: Monsoon season changes the water
things_to_know.note: The wave dataset's biggest-month reading is September (1.24 m mean, up to 2.12 m); IBTrACS records 7 tropical cyclone tracks near Kamala over 50 years, peak Category 3 — treat May–October swimming with more caution.

things_to_know.label: Beach length is disputed in sources
things_to_know.note: Wikipedia gives 3 km; Phuket101 gives 2 km. Both describe the same stretch; the discrepancy has not been resolved in public sources.

access_note: Kamala sits on Phuket's west coast, in Kathu District. By road it is roughly 25 km (about 30 minutes) from Phuket International Airport (HKT) via Highway 402 (Thepkrasattri Road) and coastal roads — the dataset's 17.8 km figure is straight-line distance, not the driving route. Patong, the nearest sizeable town, is about 10 km by road (6.9 km straight-line). No rail or ferry service reaches Kamala directly; taxis, songthaews, and rental vehicles are the practical options.
